tips.title: Correlation is not cause
tips.body:
Two things moving together does not mean one makes the other happen. Ice cream sales and drowning both rise in summer; neither causes the other, and the **hot weather** behind both is called a third factor.

The exam asks this as *"does this prove that…?"* The answer is always **no**, followed by a reason: the data shows a **relationship**, not a **cause**.

tips.title: Inside is safe, outside is not
tips.body:
**Interpolating** means reading inside the range of the data you have. It is reasonably safe, because the pattern was measured there.

**Extrapolating** means reading beyond the end of the data. It assumes the trend carries on, and there is no evidence that it does.

In, safe. Out, risky.

tips.title: Read the question for which variable is which
tips.body:
The thing that is **changed or chosen** goes on the **x-axis**, and the thing that is **measured** goes on the y-axis. Hours revised is chosen; the mark follows.

Get them the wrong way round and every reading is wrong, even though the graph looks fine.

tips.title: Does your line have points either side?
tips.body:
A line of best fit is drawn **by eye**, following the trend, with **roughly as many points above it as below**. It does **not** have to pass through the origin, and it does **not** join the first and last points.

If every point sits on one side of your line, it is in the wrong place.

tips.title: Name the correlation in two words
tips.body:
Strength then direction: **strong positive**, **weak negative**, or **no correlation**. Two words earn the mark where "it goes up" does not.

And in context: *the more hours revised, the higher the mark* says the same thing in the language of the question, which is what an *interpret* question wants.

why.matters:
Almost every claim you meet outside a classroom is really a claim about two things moving together: screen time and sleep, exercise and blood pressure, a fertiliser and a crop. A scatter graph is how that kind of claim is drawn, and the line of best fit is how a prediction is squeezed out of it.

It is also where the most common misreading in public life lives. Two things rising together is evidence of a relationship and nothing more, and most of the work in this topic is learning to say exactly that, and to know how far a line can be trusted before it starts inventing numbers.

examples.title: The revision graph, and the trap in it
examples.body:
Twelve students recorded their revision hours and their test mark. The points climb from left to right: more revision, higher mark, which is **positive correlation**.

The line of best fit rises about **5 marks for every extra hour**, and meets the mark axis near **31** — roughly what someone scores with no revision at all.

Now the trap. Follow the line out to **20 hours** and it predicts **131 marks** on a paper marked out of **100**. Nothing has gone wrong with the arithmetic; the line has simply been used outside the data it was drawn from. That is extrapolation, and this is why the specification asks you to know its dangers.

visual.alt: The same scatter graph of test mark against hours of revision, with a straight line of best fit drawn through the points, rising about 5 marks for each extra hour and meeting the mark axis near 31

examples.title: Two things that rise together, and one that does not cause the other
examples.body:
Across a summer, ice cream sales and the number of people who drown both rise. Plot one against the other and you get a convincing positive correlation.

No one thinks ice cream causes drowning. **Hot weather** causes both: more ice cream sold, and more people swimming. A cause behind both is what makes the correlation appear.

That is the whole shape of the exam question. You are shown a real correlation and asked whether it proves a cause. It never does, and the mark is for saying why: something else could be behind both.

steps.title: Two measurements on the same thing
steps.body:
Everything in this topic starts with **bivariate data**: **two** measurements taken from each member of a group.

Twelve students, and for each one the hours they revised **and** the mark they got. Each student becomes one **point**: hours across, mark up.

The variable that is chosen or set goes on the **x-axis**, and the one that is measured goes on the **y-axis**. Here, hours revised is chosen and the mark follows, so hours is x.

Once plotted, the useful question is no longer about any one student. It is about the **shape of the whole cloud of points**.

steps.title: Naming the correlation
steps.body:
**Correlation** is the word for a relationship between the two variables, and it is described in **two words**: strength, then direction.

- **Positive correlation** — as one goes up, so does the other. The cloud slopes **up** to the right.
- **Negative correlation** — as one goes up, the other goes down. The cloud slopes **down** to the right.
- **No correlation** — no slope worth speaking of. The points are scattered with no trend.

And the strength:

- **Strong** — the points sit close to a line.
- **Weak** — there is a trend, but the points are spread widely around it.

The revision graph is **strong positive** correlation.

**Say it in context too.** *The more hours a student revised, the higher their mark* is what an *interpret* question wants; “it goes up” is not.

steps.title: The line of best fit
steps.body:
A **line of best fit** is a single straight line drawn **by eye** through the trend. The specification calls it an *estimated* line, and that word is doing work: there is no calculation, and two sensible people will draw slightly different lines.

What makes a line right:

- It follows the **direction of the trend**.
- It has **roughly as many points above it as below**.
- It is a **single straight line**, drawn with a ruler, across the range of the data.

What loses marks:

- **Joining the first and last points.** That uses two of the twelve and ignores the rest.
- **Forcing it through the origin.** Only do that if the context demands it — here it would mean no revision gives no marks, which the data says is false.
- **Drawing a curve**, or a line that zigzags between points.

For the revision data a reasonable line rises about **5 marks per hour** and crosses the mark axis near **31**.

steps.body: The line is only useful once you read something off it. The method is the same every time, and the last step is the one that earns the marks.

From the line, go straight across to the **mark** axis and read the value.
6 hours is **inside** the range of the data, which runs from 2 to 12 hours.
steps.note: Reading inside the data is called interpolation.

steps.text: So the estimate is **reasonably reliable** — though it is still an estimate, because the points are scattered about the line rather than on it.

steps.title: Interpolation, extrapolation, and the danger
steps.body:
The specification asks you to *interpolate and extrapolate apparent trends while knowing the dangers of so doing*. Both words, and the danger.

**Interpolation** is reading **inside** the range of the data. The revision data runs from 2 to 12 hours, so any reading between those is interpolation, and reasonably safe: the trend was actually measured there.

**Extrapolation** is reading **beyond** the data. It assumes the trend keeps going, and nothing in the data says it does.

The revision line makes the danger obvious. Extend it to **20 hours** and it predicts **131 marks** on a paper marked out of **100**. The arithmetic is right; the line has been asked a question the data cannot answer.

> A prediction is only as good as the range it came from, and a line does not know where its data stopped.

Real trends flatten, bend or reverse outside the range that was measured. Revision has diminishing returns; a plant stops growing however much fertiliser it is given.

steps.title: Correlation is not causation
steps.body:
This is the sentence the specification names, and it is worth having word for word: **correlation does not indicate causation**.

A correlation says the two things **move together**. It does not say one **makes** the other happen. Three things could be going on:

- **A causes B.** More revision really does raise the mark.
- **B causes A.** The arrow points the other way from the one assumed.
- **A third factor causes both.** Ice cream sales and drownings rise together because of the **weather**.

And with a small sample, a fourth: **coincidence**.

**How the question is asked.** *“A newspaper says this proves that owning more books makes children cleverer. Comment on this.”* The answer has two halves, and both are needed:

1. Say what the data **does** show: a positive correlation.
2. Say what it **does not** show: that one causes the other, because a third factor — here a home with more books may also be one with more help and time to read — could explain both.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**1.** A scatter graph of a car's mileage against its price slopes down, with the points quite spread out. Describe the correlation in two words, and then in context.

**2.** A line of best fit has equation y = 5x + 31. Estimate y when x = 4.

**3.** The data behind that line covers x from 2 to 12. A student uses it to find y when x = 25. Name what they have done and say why the answer should not be trusted.

**4.** A report says that towns with more libraries have lower crime. Explain why this does not show that libraries reduce crime.

**Answers.** 1. **Weak negative** correlation: the higher the mileage, the lower the price, but the points are spread so the relationship is not tight. 2. $5 \times 4 + 31 = 51$. 3. **Extrapolation** — reading beyond the range of the data, so it assumes a trend that was never measured there. 4. It shows a **correlation**, not a cause. A **third factor**, such as the size or wealth of the town, could affect both the number of libraries and the crime rate.

steps.title: Going deeper: outliers, and what a line cannot tell you
steps.body:
**Outliers.** One point well away from the trend is an **outlier**. On the revision graph, the student who revised for 5 hours and scored 49 sits below the others at that point.

You are not allowed to delete it because it is inconvenient. What you can say is:

- it may be a **recording error**, worth checking; or
- it may be **genuine** — that student was ill, or had studied the wrong thing.

A single outlier **pulls a by-eye line towards it**, so it is worth noticing before drawing.

**What the line cannot tell you.** Even a strong correlation with a tidy line leaves three things unsaid:

- **Nothing about any individual.** The line gives the trend; a particular student may sit far off it.
- **Nothing outside the range.** See extrapolation.
- **Nothing about cause.** See above, and expect to be asked.

**The mean point.** A line of best fit should pass through the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ — the mean of the x values and the mean of the y values. For the revision data that is about $(7, 65)$. Plotting it first and drawing the line through it is the quickest way to get a by-eye line in a defensible place.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Bivariate data** is two measurements from each member of a group; each becomes one **point**.
- The variable **chosen** goes on the **x-axis**, the one **measured** on the y-axis.
- **Correlation** is described in two words: **strength** then **direction**.
- **Positive** slopes up, **negative** slopes down, **no correlation** has no trend.
- **Strong** means the points hug a line; **weak** means they are spread around it.
- Say it **in context** as well: *the more x, the higher y*.
- A **line of best fit** is drawn **by eye**, straight, following the trend, with **roughly as many points above as below**.
- Do **not** join the first and last points, and do **not** force it through the origin.
- It should pass through the **mean point** $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
- **Interpolation** reads **inside** the data: reasonably reliable.
- **Extrapolation** reads **outside** it: unreliable, because the trend is assumed, not measured.
- On this data, 20 hours predicts **131 marks** out of 100 — the danger, in one number.
- **Correlation does not indicate causation.** A third factor may cause both.
- An **outlier** is noticed and explained, not deleted.

questions.prompt: A gardener records the amount of fertiliser given to 15 tomato plants and the mass of tomatoes each plant produced. The scatter graph shows strong positive correlation for amounts between 10 g and 50 g of fertiliser. The gardener concludes that giving 200 g of fertiliser will produce an enormous crop, and that fertiliser causes growth. Comment on both conclusions.
questions.solution:
The first conclusion extrapolates. The data covers 10 g to 50 g of fertiliser, and 200 g is far outside that range, so the prediction assumes the trend continues where nothing was measured. Real trends rarely continue indefinitely: the yield is likely to flatten off, and too much fertiliser can damage a plant, so the crop could be smaller rather than enormous.

The second conclusion confuses correlation with causation. The graph shows that the amount of fertiliser and the mass of tomatoes rise together, which is a correlation. It does not on its own show that the fertiliser causes the growth. A third factor could be behind both: the plants that were given more fertiliser may also have been the better-tended ones, getting more water and more light as well.

To support the causal claim the gardener would need a controlled experiment, keeping water, light and soil the same and varying only the fertiliser.

questions.prompt: Twelve students recorded their hours of revision, from 2 to 12 hours, and their mark out of 100. A line of best fit has equation y = 5x + 31. Explain what the gradient and the intercept of this line mean in the context of the data, and explain why the intercept should be treated with caution.
questions.solution:
The gradient of the line is 5, and on this graph y is the mark and x is the hours of revision. So the gradient is the change in mark for each extra hour: on average, a student who revises for one hour longer scores about 5 marks more.

The intercept is 31, which is the value of y when x is zero. In context that is the mark the line predicts for a student who did no revision at all: about 31 out of 100.

That second figure needs caution. The data collected covers 2 to 12 hours, so x = 0 lies outside it: no student in the sample did no revision. Reading the line there is extrapolation, and it assumes the straight-line trend continues below 2 hours when nothing was measured to show that it does. The intercept is a property of the line, not a finding about students who do not revise.

examTechnique.body:
Describe correlation in two words, strength then direction, and then say it again in the words of the question. “Strong positive” earns the first mark; “the more hours revised, the higher the mark” earns the interpretation mark.

Draw a line of best fit with a ruler, straight, following the trend, with roughly as many points above it as below. Do not join the first and last points, and do not force it through the origin unless the context says zero gives zero.

When reading a value off the line, draw the lines on the graph. Examiners give method marks for the construction lines even when the reading is slightly out.

Name interpolation and extrapolation when asked how reliable a prediction is, and say which range the data covered. A prediction outside that range is unreliable because the trend is assumed rather than measured.

For any “does this prove” question, answer in two halves: what the data does show (a correlation) and what it does not (a cause), then offer a third factor that could explain both.
examinerErrors: Giving only the direction — “positive” — when the question asks you to describe the correlation, which wants the strength too.
Describing the correlation but never putting it in the context of the question.
Joining the first and last points instead of drawing a line of best fit through the trend.
Forcing the line through the origin when the data does not go there.
Reading from the points rather than from the line of best fit.
Using the line far outside the range of the data and not saying that this is unreliable.
Concluding that one variable causes the other from a correlation alone.
Deleting an outlier rather than identifying it and commenting on what might explain it.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the line of best fit as an estimate and says so: it gives a prediction, then says how far it can be trusted and why, naming interpolation or extrapolation and the range the data actually covered. Asked to interpret a gradient or an intercept, it puts both into the units of the question — marks per hour, and the mark at zero hours — and notices when the intercept is itself an extrapolation. On any claim about cause it answers in two halves, stating what the correlation does show before saying what it does not, and it names a plausible third factor rather than asserting that none exists. It notices an outlier before drawing the line, because a by-eye line is pulled towards one, and it comments on the outlier rather than removing it.
